item.title: Global-scale variability of glacier velocity and mass loss across terminus environments
item.dc:creator: Joseph Mallalieu, Jonathan Lee Carrivick, Matthias Huss, Iestyn David Barr, Nicholas E. Barrand, Cassandra L. Raby
item.description:
Nature Communications — matched: glacier, mass loss, sea level, sea-level rise
Abstract The environment in which a glacier terminates can strongly influence its behaviour, stability and future evolution, yet the relationship between terminus type and glacier dynamics at the global scale remains poorly constrained. Here we present a globally-complete classification of glacier termini distinguishing between land, lake, marine and shelf environments, and integrate it with datasets of glacier geometry, dynamics and climate. We show that although lake-, marine- and shelf-terminating glaciers comprise only 3.2% of glaciers globally, they account for over half of global glacier area and mass loss. We also show that lake- and marine-terminating glaciers flow, on average, 10% and 44% faster than land-terminating glaciers, respectively. Furthermore, specific (area-normalised) mass loss rates at lake-terminating glaciers are 57% greater than those at land- and marine-terminating glaciers. Our findings underscore the need for improved representation of non-land glacier termini in models of glacier evolution and sea-level rise, and suggest that distinguishing the environmental and geometric controls of termini on glacier dynamics remains an important challenge for future research.

item.title: A conceptual model of seasonal groundwater storage and meltwater transfer through a frontal moraine in the Chilean semiarid Andes (30°S)
item.dc:creator: Gonzalo Navarro, Shelley A. MacDonell, Rémi Valois, Giulia De Pasquale, Benjamin Aubrey Robson, Christophe Kinnard
item.description:
Geomorphology — matched: cryosphere, glacier, meltwater, remote sensing
The hydrology of (semi)arid Andean regions is strongly controlled by the cryosphere, particularly debris-free glaciers and snowmelt. Glacial systems are commonly connected to proglacial landforms, an interaction that determines the fate of meltwater by storing and transferring it to the wider catchment. This study investigates the hydrological role of a frontal moraine in regulating water delivery from the glacial system to the proglacial stream and the downstream environment. We combined surface-based geophysics, multi-temporal remote sensing and hydrological monitoring to characterise the internal structure and seasonal surface water dynamics of a moraine in the frontal area of the Tapado glacier complex, Chilean semiarid Andes. Geophysical observations suggest that the investigated area of the moraine is not dominated by glacial ice but instead consists predominantly of detrital material with high near-surface water content and deep high-resistivity zones consistent with limited seasonal interstitial ice mixed with unfrozen water. Surface water analyses on and in the immediate surroundings of the moraine showed that surface water is highly seasonal. Surface water observations indicate that pond growth during the early ablation season is consistent with limited infiltration due to seasonal interstitial ice at depth, whereas progressive pond drainage and changes in the proglacial stream signal suggest increasingly efficient subsurface water connectivity and water-transfer later in the season. Together, these observations support a conceptual model in which the moraine temporarily stores groundwater during the early ablation season and progressively increases subsurface connectivity as seasonal interstitial ice degrades, thereby regulating the timing of meltwater transfer toward the proglacial spring and stream. Our results highlight the importance of proglacial moraines as active groundwater storage and transfer components in deglaciating catchments and emphasize the need for targeted hydrological characterisation and monitoring from these landforms to better constrain current and future water availability in cryosphere-dependent mountain regions.

item.title: Integrating a global glacier model into local hydrological modeling: Impacts on melt contributions
item.dc:creator: Justine Berg, Pascal Horton, Martina Kauzlaric, Alexandra von der Esch, Bettina Schaefli
item.description:
Hydrology and earth system sciences — matched: glacier, meltwater, climate change
Abstract. Snow and glacier meltwater are critical water resources for mountain regions, yet their accurate representation in hydrological models remains challenging. As climate change alters the timing and magnitude of melt contributions, accurate partitioning between snow and glacier sources becomes increasingly important. To address this challenge, this study couples the hydrological model HBV (as implemented in the Raven modeling framework) with the Global Glacier Evolution Model GloGEM and integrates a snow redistribution scheme for application across 14 glaciated headwater catchments in Switzerland. At this local catchment scale, we investigate whether glacier constraints and the addition of snow redistribution reduce parameter equifinality and increase the reliability of melt contribution estimates. Simulations are evaluated against observed streamflow, gridded snow water equivalent data, and glacier melt data based on observed mass balance. The gravitational snow redistribution algorithm successfully prevents unrealistic high-elevation snow accumulation and improves catchment average SWE simulation performance. Uncoupled HBV configurations outperform coupled HBV-GloGEM setups according to streamflow metrics. However, this superior performance is achieved by simulating glacier melt rates exceeding GloGEM estimates and glacier storage change data by factors of 2–3 in some catchments, effectively using glacier ice to offset precipitation biases in forcing data, which can be critical for climate change impact studies. Glacier melt contributions can vary by nearly an order of magnitude among best-performing parameter sets, highlighting severe parameter equifinality. Coupling with GloGEM, calibrated using glacier-specific geodetic mass balance, produces glacier melt consistent with observations and substantially improves identifiability of both glacier and snowmelt contributions. Despite lower streamflow performance metrics, glacier melt constraints prevent compensatory errors that would compromise projections as melt dynamics shift under climate change. Applying this framework to future climate scenarios and integrating additional constraints such as snow observations may further improve the reliability of melt contribution projections.
